title: Language: Deceptive, Yet Creative
note: Scripture quotations are from the Berean Standard Bible (public domain) unless otherwise noted.

paragraphs: A memory researcher once showed groups of people the same film of a car accident and asked how fast the cars were going, changing just one word: one group was asked about cars that “contacted” each other, another about cars that “smashed” into each other. The “smashed” group gave higher speeds, and a week later they remembered broken glass that was never in the film. One word wrote a false memory into people’s minds.

Language is not a clear pane of glass. It’s a lens. A surgery after which “ninety percent of patients survive” sounds different from one after which “ten percent die,” even though it’s the same information. Whoever arranges the words quietly arranges our thinking. And deception starts closer to home than advertising: with labels. “Lazy.” “Crybaby.” “You always.” A label doesn’t describe behavior; it describes a person, and it works like a verdict: a child who keeps being called clumsy eventually comes to agree. Words are like feathers scattered in the wind: you can’t gather them back up.

Yet that same power also builds. For many people, sincere appreciation is the main way they receive love. Marriage researchers have found that in lasting relationships, every unpleasant exchange is outweighed several times over by kind ones. The book of Proverbs put it this way three thousand years earlier: a gentle answer turns away wrath, and pleasant words are healing to the bones.

In practice: run your words through three sieves, the sieve of truth, of necessity, and of kindness. Swap labels for descriptions: instead of “You’re such a slob,” say “Your backpack has been lying on the floor for three days.” Once a day, say one specific good word to someone close to you. And watch the words you use about yourself, because a label you stick on yourself works the same way as one stuck on a child, and simply putting a feeling into words takes away some of its power.

The Bible begins with a word that creates the world. Our words create worlds too, small, household ones: the atmosphere at the table, a child’s picture of himself. James compared the tongue to the rudder of a great ship and to the spark that sets a forest ablaze. So choose your words the way you would choose between life and death, because that is exactly what’s at stake.

quote.text: Life and death are in the power of the tongue, and those who love it will eat its fruit.

questions: What sentence you heard in childhood do you still carry with you today?
Who around you has long been waiting for a kind word that’s in your heart but that you haven’t said yet?

paragraphs: In the 1970s, an American memory researcher conducted an experiment that is still striking today. Groups of people were shown the same short film of a car accident and then asked the same question about the cars’ speed, with only one word changed. Some were asked how fast the cars were going when they “contacted” each other; others, how fast they were going when they “smashed” into each other. The “smashed” group gave noticeably higher speeds. But the real surprise came a week later. Asked whether they had seen any broken glass in the film, people in the “smashed” group said yes much more often. There was no broken glass in the film. These people weren’t lying. Their memory had simply been rewritten by one word, quietly and without their knowledge. A single word added something to their memory that they had never seen.

That is the first thing to understand about language: it is not a clear pane of glass through which we look at the world. It is a lens that shapes that world before we have time to think. The same surgery described as “ninety percent of patients survive” sounds encouraging, while described as “ten percent of patients die” it stirs up fear, even though both versions say exactly the same thing. The same tax gained or lost support depending on whether it was called an estate tax or a death tax. Stores know that “marked down from $399 to $199” works better than the $199 price alone. Whoever arranges the words quietly arranges our thinking. Headlines live by this principle: “wave,” “shock,” “scandal” are words chosen not to describe the world but to stop a thumb scrolling down a screen. That’s why it pays to listen carefully not only to what we’re told, but to how it has been labeled, and with every strongly worded piece of news to ask yourself a simple question: how would the same sentence sound if it were phrased calmly?

But the deceptiveness of language starts much closer to home than politics and advertising. It starts at home, with labels. “Lazy.” “Crybaby.” “You always.” “You never.” A label differs from a description in that it doesn’t speak about behavior; it speaks about the person, and that’s why it works like a verdict. A child who is told again and again that he is clumsy doesn’t hear information about spilled milk. He hears information about himself, and after a while he starts to agree with it, and then to behave accordingly. Adults are no more immune: married couples can carry a single sentence spoken in anger inside them for years. Gossip works the same way. An old comparison says that words are like feathers shaken out of a pillow into the wind: however much you want to, you can’t gather them back up.

There is one more listener we forget most often: ourselves. Each of us carries on a constant inner monologue, and the words of that monologue work exactly the same way as words spoken out loud. Someone who tells himself “I’m hopeless” after every mistake sticks a label on himself just as effectively as he would on a child, and over time he starts living by its dictates. The same mistake described with the sentence “I handled that badly; next time I’ll start differently” leaves a person with a task, not a verdict. Psychologists have also discovered something surprising: simply putting a feeling into words takes away some of its power. Telling yourself “I feel angry” or “This is fear” engages a brake in the brain that no amount of teeth-gritting can engage. So a word can be first aid: name what you’re feeling, and by doing so you’re already beginning to master it.

Speaking of labels, it’s worth knowing that even praise can be a trap. Research on children has shown that praising talent, for example, “You’re so smart,” has the opposite effect from the one intended: children praised this way start avoiding difficult tasks, because they’re afraid of losing the title of “smart.” Children praised for effort and specific actions, for example, “I can see you worked on that for a long time and didn’t give up,” choose harder tasks and grow faster. The difference is purely linguistic, and the effects last for years.

But the same power that wounds can also build, and that is the second, brighter half of the truth about language. For many people, a kind word is the main way they receive love: relationship researchers have described how some of us feel loved above all when we hear sincere appreciation, and no amount of gifts or favors can replace it. Marriage researchers, for their part, have found that in lasting, healthy relationships, every unpleasant exchange is outweighed several times over by kind ones, and when the ratio flips, the relationship starts to die. The book of Proverbs said the same thing more briefly, three thousand years earlier: a gentle answer turns away wrath, and pleasant words are a honeycomb, sweet to the soul and healing to the bones. Notice that: healing to the bones. The author of that sentence knew nothing about stress hormones, and yet he wrote that a kind word heals the body.

There is one more principle every master communicator knows: what counts is not what you say, but what the other person hears. Between your intention and the way it’s received lies the whole space of that person’s associations, fears, and experiences. You can speak the truth in a way that sounds like an attack, and you can say a hard thing in a way that sounds like care. Someone who speaks out of concern for the listener, and not to show off how much they know, is practicing more than a technique. They are practicing service.

What can you do about this in practice? First, run your words through three sieves before you let them out: Is it true? Is it necessary? Is it kind? A sentence that doesn’t pass through any of the sieves usually doesn’t need to be said. Second, swap labels for descriptions. Instead of “You’re such a slob,” say “Your backpack has been lying on the floor for three days.” A description leaves the other person room; a label closes it off. Third, once a day, say one specific good word to one person close to you. Not a generic “You’re awesome,” but something you actually noticed: “I saw how patiently you explained that homework to our little one.” Specifics prove that you’re really paying attention, and it’s specifics that build people up. Fourth, watch the words you use about yourself: after a mistake, describe the behavior; don’t pass a verdict on the person. Fifth, try a one-week no-complaining experiment and watch what happens to your own mood, because words shape not only the listeners. They also shape the speaker. And one more thing, to get you started: think of someone you owe something to, and tell them so directly, or write them a few sentences. People can carry words like that with them for decades, and they cost the writer five minutes. If you want to see this power in your own life, try one more exercise: write down three sentences you heard in childhood that you still carry today. For most people, the list will include one that lifts them up and one that has weighed them down for decades. That’s the best proof of how long a single sentence keeps working, and the best reason to choose your own sentences with care.

sections.heading: Summary
paragraphs: Language doesn’t describe the world neutrally; it helps create it: a single word in a question can plant a false memory in people’s minds, and the same information phrased differently leads to different decisions. This power cuts both ways. Labels like “lazy” or “you always” work like verdicts and can shape a person for years, while sincere, specific appreciation builds a person up just as lastingly; in good marriages, kind exchanges far outweigh critical ones. The same mechanics apply to our inner monologue: labels we stick on ourselves shape us just as much as those we stick on others, and simply putting a feeling into words takes away some of its power. Everyday practice: three sieves before every difficult sentence, the sieves of truth, necessity, and kindness; descriptions instead of labels, including toward yourself; praise for effort, not talent; one specific good word a day for someone close to you; and a week without complaining, to see what your own words do to the speaker.

sections.heading: Look Higher
paragraphs: The Bible begins with a word that creates. “God said,” and there was light, sea, life. Then the text adds that human beings were made in the image of God, and perhaps it’s no coincidence that we are the only creatures that speak. Our words create worlds too, only small, household ones: the atmosphere at the table, a child’s picture of himself, the climate of a marriage for years to come. Nor is it a coincidence that when God wants to transform a person, He so often starts by changing the word that person is called by: Abram becomes Abraham, father of a multitude, long before the promised son is born to him, and wavering Simon is named Peter, the rock, long before he starts behaving like a rock. The new name goes first, and the life grows into it. The apostle James compared the tongue to a rudder that, though small, steers a great ship, and to a spark that sets a forest ablaze. Jesus said that out of the overflow of the heart the mouth speaks, so our words are also a diagnosis: by what comes out of us, we can tell what lives in us. And the book of Proverbs summed up this whole teaching in one sentence that psychology has yet to improve on:

quote.text: Life and death are in the power of the tongue, and those who love it will eat its fruit.
